disclaimer: Proxy inspired by the six-kinds-of-work model popularized by Patrick Lencioni (Wonder, Invention, Discernment, Galvanizing, Enablement, Tenacity). Not the licensed Working Genius assessment; every item here is original wording written from the public description of the six categories.

scale.prompt_suffix: One to five: one is 'drains me', three is neutral, five is 'really energizes me'.

competency_scale.prompt_suffix: Not at all, a little, somewhat, mostly, or completely?

wonder.name: Wonder
wonder.description: Pondering possibility and potential; noticing what could be better and asking why.

invention.name: Invention
invention.description: Coming up with original ideas and novel solutions to problems.

discernment.name: Discernment
discernment.description: Evaluating ideas with instinct and judgment; sensing which ones have legs.

galvanizing.name: Galvanizing
galvanizing.description: Inspiring and organizing people to take action on an idea.

enablement.name: Enablement
enablement.description: Providing help and support when it's needed, in whatever form it's needed.

tenacity.name: Tenacity
tenacity.description: Pushing work through to completion and making sure it achieves the result.

bands.competency: middle 2: can do it, neutral on energy

scoring_notes: Energy score per type = mean of its 3 energy items on 1-5, mapped to 0-100 as (mean - 1) / 4 * 100. Competency score = the single competency item, same mapping. Types are ranked by energy, ties broken by competency, then by bank order. Ranks 1-2 are genius, 3-4 competency, 5-6 frustration. Confidence = the smaller of the two gaps that define the bands (rank 2 vs 3, rank 4 vs 5), 10 points = full, times a coverage factor. Notes flag types with high competency but low energy (burnout risk) and high energy but low competency (worth developing). See scoring.ts.

items.text: Sitting with a big open question, like 'what could this business become', with no need to answer it yet.
Noticing that something in how we work isn't quite right, and wondering out loud why nobody has looked at it.
Spending a whole afternoon exploring possibilities with no deliverable at the end.
Being handed a blank page and asked to come up with something that doesn't exist yet.
Brainstorming ten different ways to solve a problem nobody has cracked.
Designing a new process, product or plan from nothing.
Being shown three rough ideas and asked which one has legs.
Giving someone honest feedback on their plan before they commit to it.
Spotting the flaw in a proposal that everyone else is excited about.
Getting a room of people fired up about an idea so they want to join in.
Reaching out to people one by one to get them on board with something new.
Being the one who says 'let's go' and pulls everyone into motion.
Someone asks for help on their project and you drop what you're doing to pitch in.
Being the person a team leans on to make things happen behind the scenes.
Noticing what a teammate needs and quietly handling it without being asked.
The last ten percent of a project: closing out every loose end until it's truly done.
Grinding through the boring part of a task because it has to get finished.
Keeping a list of open items and driving each one to closed.
People tell me I ask the questions nobody else thought to ask.
I'm genuinely good at coming up with original ideas.
My gut calls about which ideas will work tend to be right.
I'm good at rallying people around a cause.
I'm reliable support. People know they can hand me things and they'll get done.
I'm good at finishing what I start, down to the last detail.
